title: The Rules for an Open Hole, and What the Owner Sees When He Walks It
summary: In American practice the OSHA excavation rules require a protective system for workers in most excavations, chosen from sloping, support or shields according to soil type. The owner walking a dig looks at the crest, the base, the water and the paperwork, and observes rather than directs.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the rules for an open excavation are workplace safety law, and they decide whether the hole can be sloped back or must be shored. When you walk the site, look first at the crest, because that is where the load is and where collapses start.

In plain English

An excavation is any hole cut into the ground; a trench is a narrow one. In the United States the governing rules are OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Excavations. They are occupational safety law, not a building code, and outside the United States local safety law governs. Every figure in this lesson is quoted as commonly cited and must be verified against the current regulation [unverified — confirm independently].

When protection is required

Workers in an excavation need a protective system unless the excavation is in stable rock, or is less than about 1.5 metres (5 feet) deep and a competent person has examined it and found no indication of potential cave-in [unverified — confirm independently]. Protective systems come in three families: sloping and benching, where the sides are cut back so the soil stands by itself; support systems, such as shoring, sheet piles or soldier piles and lagging; and shields, steel boxes that protect workers inside them. Beyond about 6 metres (20 feet) deep, the protective system must be designed by a registered professional engineer [unverified — confirm independently].

Soil types and slopes

Appendix A classifies soil as stable rock, Type A, Type B or Type C, with Type A the most cohesive and Type C the least, including granular soils and submerged or seeping soil. Soil that is wet or seeping is classed as Type C, whatever it would be when dry. Appendix B gives maximum allowable slopes for excavations under about 6 metres: commonly quoted as three-quarters to one for Type A, one to one for Type B, and one and a half to one for Type C, expressed as horizontal to vertical [unverified — confirm independently].

Other rules worth remembering

Spoil and equipment kept at least about 0.6 metres (2 feet) back from the edge; a safe means of egress, such as a ladder, within about 7.6 metres (25 feet) of travel in trenches about 1.2 metres (4 feet) deep or more; and daily inspection, and after any rain or other hazard-increasing event, by a competent person with authority to stop work [unverified — confirm independently]. In the building code, IBC Chapters 18 and 33 add requirements on the lateral support of existing footings and protection of adjoining property during excavation [unverified — confirm independently].

A worked example

Suppose a hypothetical excavation 3 metres deep in clay that is seeping groundwater at the base.

  1. Dry, the clay might classify as Type A or B. Seeping, it is Type C.
  2. Type C at one and a half to one: 3 metres deep needs 1.5 times 3, which is 4.5 metres of horizontal setback from the toe to the crest, on every side.
  3. The building's footprint sits 3 metres from the site boundary on one side. A 4.5 metre slope does not fit: it would cut 1.5 metres into the neighbour's land.
  4. So on that side a support system is required, designed by an engineer, whatever its cost compared with sloping. Shoring has become a geometry decision, not a cost decision.
  5. On the open sides, sloping may still be cheaper. A hybrid is common: shored where the boundary forces it, sloped where there is room. Tomorrow's lesson prices that choice.

The dig, in sequence

A typical sequence protects the survey control, strips topsoil, digs in bulk, then takes the last layer to formation carefully, by a smooth bucket rather than teeth, and seals it with blinding concrete the same day it is exposed. The last few hundred millimetres decide the bearing surface: exposed formation softens in rain, dries and cracks in sun, and is churned by plant. Working platforms for piling rigs and cranes, and access ramps, look like nothing but gravel and are designed elements; a platform failure drops the machine.

What the owner looks at

Walk the crest first: no spoil or plant on the lip, and no loaded machine near the edge. Then the base: no standing water, and the formation not churned or softened. Then the water: the standby pump present and connected, the alarm reaching a named person, the discharge going somewhere lawful, because silt into a public drain is a regulatory event in the owner's name. Then the paperwork: yesterday's competent-person inspection record, and the name of today's competent person. Ask one question aloud every visit: what is today's groundwater level? If nobody can answer, nobody is reading the instruments.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is load at the crest: spoil, a stockpile or plant close to the edge is a common contributing cause of excavation collapse, because it adds weight exactly where the soil is least supported.

The beginner's mistake

Under Design-Build, the beginner gives an instruction on site, "move that spoil heap", which feels responsible. Directing method moves temporary works responsibility back onto the owner. Observe, photograph, write, and ask the contractor to confirm compliance in writing; do not direct.

How you will use it

Before award, require the temporary works design for the excavation as a named deliverable with a named designer and an independent check. On site, walk the crest, base, water and paperwork in that order, and record what you see. Professional sign-off required: a registered professional engineer for protective systems beyond the regulatory threshold, and the contractor's competent person daily.
checklist: Keep spoil and plant back from the crest; a loaded machine on the lip is a stop-and-ask moment.
Check the base for standing water and a churned or softened formation.
Confirm blinding is placed the same day the formation is exposed.
Check the standby pump, the alarm reaching a named person, and lawful discharge.
Ask to see yesterday's competent-person inspection record and today's named competent person.
Ask aloud on every visit for today's groundwater level.
Require the excavation temporary works design as a named, independently checked deliverable.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: Your excavation is 3 metres deep in clay that seeps at the base, and the boundary is 3 metres from the face on one side. Can you slope that side?
selftest.a: No. Seeping soil is classed as Type C, which under the commonly quoted OSHA Appendix B slope of one and a half to one needs about 4.5 metres of setback at 3 metres deep (verify against the current regulation). That does not fit within 3 metres of the boundary, so that side needs an engineered support system. Shoring there is a geometry decision, not a cost choice.

apply: For a hypothetical 2.5 metre deep excavation, write the required setback for each of Types A, B and C using the commonly quoted slopes, and mark which would need shoring if the boundary were 3 metres away.
sources: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P and Appendices A and B as commonly cited; IBC Chapters 18 and 33 on adjoining property. All thresholds and slopes are to be verified against the current regulation and adopted code edition [unverified — confirm independently]. Example hypothetical.

title: Sloped or Shored: Pricing the Shape of the Hole
summary: A shored hole is base area times depth, while a sloped hole needs the prismoidal formula and comes out much larger. The extra volume also has to come back as backfill, takes more trucks and more days, and enlarges the area to dewater.
body:
Mr Shabazz, shoring has a visible price and sloping has a hidden one. Measure both in cubic metres, truck loads and days before you decide which is cheaper.

In plain English

Volume decides the cost of digging, haulage, disposal and backfill. A vertical-sided, shored hole is simple: its volume is its base area times its depth. A sloped hole is wider at the top than at the bottom, so it holds far more soil. Everything removed beyond the building's own footprint has to be carted away and, later, brought back and compacted around the foundations.

The formulas

Always start from the footprint plus working space, the gap the crews need to form and waterproof foundations, often about a metre each side; ask what allowance the contractor used. For a shored hole, volume equals base area times depth. For a sloped hole, use the prismoidal formula: volume equals the bottom area, plus four times the mid-depth area, plus the top area, all times the depth, divided by six. The mid-depth area is measured halfway up the slope.

Soil also bulks when it is dug: loose spoil occupies more volume than it did in the ground. A bulking factor, often quoted around 1.2 to 1.3 for many soils, converts bank volume to the loose volume trucks actually carry; confirm it for your soil [unverified — confirm independently].

A worked example

Take a hypothetical footprint of 40 by 24 metres, dug 2.5 metres deep in Type C soil.

  1. Add 1 metre of working space each side: the base becomes 42 by 26 metres, an area of 1,092 square metres.
  2. Shored: 1,092 times 2.5 equals 2,730 cubic metres in the ground.
  3. Sloped at one and a half to one: the setback is 1.5 times 2.5, which is 3.75 metres each side. The top is 49.5 by 33.5 metres, which is 1,658.25 square metres, about 52 percent larger than the base.
  4. Mid-depth: the setback is half, 1.875 metres each side, so 45.75 by 29.75 metres, which is about 1,361.06 square metres.
  5. Prismoidal volume: 1,092 plus 4 times 1,361.06 plus 1,658.25 equals about 8,194.5; times 2.5 divided by 6 gives about 3,414 cubic metres.
  6. The sloped hole removes about 684 cubic metres more, about 25 percent, and those 684 cubic metres must later return as compacted backfill.
  7. Haulage: at a bulking factor of 1.25, shored is about 3,413 cubic metres loose, sloped about 4,268. At 10 cubic metres a truck, that is about 342 loads against 427.
  8. Days: at 24 loads a day through one gate, about 14 days against 18. Haulage, not the excavator, sets the duration.
  9. Dewatering: if the water table sits within the excavation, the area to keep dry at the water level grows with the slope, often by a third or more on these dimensions, and pumping grows with it.

Comparing the two honestly

Shoring costs money you can see: the system, its design and checking, installation and removal. Sloping costs money you have to calculate: extra excavation, extra haulage and disposal, extra imported or reused backfill and its compaction testing, a larger dewatered area, more land occupied during the work, and, above all, extra days at the weekly time cost of the site. With the combined weekly cost of time from Week Two at, say, 60,000, four extra haulage days, at five working days a week, are worth about 48,000 before the backfill is counted.

The boundary often decides for you. Where the setback a slope needs is wider than the distance to the boundary, that side must be shored, and the hybrid volume falls between the two figures. Compare the options with local rates, and add the cost of the days.

Backfill is not free soil

Backfill placed against foundations must be suitable material, placed in compacted layers and tested, because poorly compacted backfill settles and takes slabs, paving and services with it. Some excavated soil is unsuitable, especially wet clay, and must be replaced with imported granular fill. Ask what proportion of the spoil the geotechnical engineer accepts for reuse. If none of it can be reused, the sloped option pays twice: once to cart the extra volume away and once to buy and import the granular fill that replaces it, with compaction tests on every layer.

Land, neighbours and the programme

A slope also occupies land for months. On a tight site the setback zone may be exactly where the crane base, the site office or the laydown area needs to go, so sloping can force a worse logistics plan and a longer programme for reasons that never appear in the earthworks price. Ask for both options to be drawn on the logistics plan before comparing them, and ask how each affects the date the foundations can start.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is comparing only the price of the shoring against the price of digging, and forgetting the time, the backfill and the dewatering. The cheaper-looking option can be the dearer one once days are priced.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner computes volume on the building footprint without working space, then is surprised by the haulage count. Always add working space first, and ask the contractor what allowance he used.

How you will use it

For each option, ask for volume in the ground, loose haulage volume, truck loads, days at the real gate rate, backfill quantity and source, and dewatered area. Price them with local rates and the weekly time cost. Let the boundary decide where it must. Professional sign-off required: temporary works designer for shoring; geotechnical engineer for slopes, bulking and backfill suitability.
checklist: Add working space to the footprint before computing any volume.
Use base area times depth for shored holes and the prismoidal formula for sloped ones.
Convert bank volume to loose volume with a bulking factor before counting trucks.
Count truck loads and days at the real gate rate; haulage sets duration.
Price the backfill, its suitability and its compaction testing.
Include the larger dewatered area of a sloped hole.
Let the boundary decide where shoring is mandatory.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A contractor quotes sloping as 40,000 cheaper than shoring. What do you ask before accepting?
selftest.a: Ask for the extra volume and its haulage days at the real gate rate, the backfill quantity and whether spoil is reusable, the extra dewatered area, and confirmation that the slope fits inside the boundary. Then price the extra days at the weekly cost of time. A sloped hole can easily cost more once time and backfill are counted.

apply: Repeat the worked example for a 30 by 20 metre footprint, 2 metres deep, with 1 metre working space, Type B slope of one to one, and compare truck loads at 10 cubic metres each.
sources: Prismoidal formula is standard earthworks practice. Slopes as commonly quoted from OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix B; bulking factors vary by soil [unverified — confirm independently]. All figures are hypothetical.

title: Dewatering: Inflow, Pumps That Survive a Weekend, and the Day the Pumps May Stop
summary: Water inflow depends on permeability, which varies so widely that only a pumping test gives a reliable figure. A pump is sized at a duty point of flow and head with standby redundancy, and dewatering may only stop once the permanent structure outweighs the water pressure beneath it.
body:
Mr Shabazz, dewatering is cheap to run and catastrophic to lose. Size it from measured permeability, buy redundancy rather than capacity, and never let the pumps stop until an engineer has certified that the structure is heavy enough to stay down.

In plain English

When an excavation goes below the water table, groundwater flows in from the sides and pushes up from below. Dewatering lowers the water level with pumps, wells or wellpoints so the work can be done dry and the base stays stable. The amount of water depends on how easily water moves through the soil, how far the water level must be lowered, and the size and shape of the excavation.

Permeability is the uncertain input

Permeability, the rate at which water moves through soil, varies enormously: from extremely low in intact clay to very high in clean sand and gravel, a range commonly described as several orders of magnitude between soil types. A calculation using a textbook value can be wrong by a factor of ten or a hundred. A pumping test, which pumps a well at a steady rate and measures how the water level falls in nearby observation wells, gives a real figure for your site. Without one, every dewatering number on the project is a guess.

Pumps: flow and head together

A pump delivers less flow the higher it must lift the water. Its performance is a curve, and the duty point is the flow it delivers at the head your system actually needs, which includes the lift plus friction losses in the pipework. A capacity quoted as flow alone, with no head, is marketing, not engineering. Ask: at what head?

The pump itself is rarely the expensive part. The expensive thing is the pump stopping. So the system is arranged with spare capacity, commonly described as N plus 1: enough pumps to handle the design flow, plus one more, with automatic standby start, an alarm that reaches a person day and night, and standby power that survives a power cut.

A worked example

Suppose a hypothetical excavation of 2,730 cubic metres, with a pumping test indicating inflow of about 20 cubic metres an hour at the required drawdown.

  1. Choose a duty point. With margin, 30 cubic metres an hour against a total head of 15 metres.
  2. Hydraulic power is water density times gravity times flow times head: 1,000 times 9.81 times 30 divided by 3,600 times 15, which is about 1,226 watts, about 1.2 kilowatts. At a pump efficiency of 60 percent, the motor needs about 2 kilowatts. Small.
  3. Now the weekend arithmetic. The site closes Friday evening and reopens Monday morning, about 60 hours; allow 72 for a long weekend. If the pumps fail Friday night, inflow of 20 cubic metres an hour times 72 hours is 1,440 cubic metres, more than half the excavation. Softened formation, flooded reinforcement, possibly a collapsed face. Redundancy and alarms are not optional.
  4. Uplift. When the permanent base slab is cast and the water level is allowed to recover, water pushes up on the slab. Suppose the base sits 2.5 metres below the recovered water level. Water pressure is about 10 kilopascals per metre of head, so about 25 kilopascals of uplift.
  5. Concrete weighs about 24 kilonewtons per cubic metre. Balancing 25 kilopascals needs 25 divided by 24, about 1.04 metres of concrete, before any factor of safety. If only 90 percent of dead load is counted, as load standards commonly require for resisting uplift, about 1.16 metres [unverified — confirm independently].
  6. A 0.5 metre slab is not enough. Dewatering must continue until enough of the structure is built to provide the remaining weight, or the slab is held down by anchors or tension piles. The engineer of record certifies that crossover point in writing before any pump is switched off.

Under Design-Build

Dewatering is usually the contractor's means and methods. The owner does not design it; he writes outcomes into the performance requirements: the required drawdown below formation, redundancy, standby power, alarms to a named person, groundwater monitoring, lawful discharge, and no cessation of pumping before written certification of the uplift crossover.

Discharge and the neighbours

Water pumped from an excavation carries silt. Discharging it into a public drain or watercourse usually needs a permit and treatment, such as settlement tanks, and doing it without one is a regulatory breach in the owner's name. Lowering the water table can also settle compressible soil under neighbouring buildings, which is why the dilapidation survey and neighbour settlement points matter.

Monitoring the water

Dewatering is managed by measurement. Piezometers or standpipes around and inside the excavation show the actual water level, and readings are taken on a stated schedule and reported with the excavation monitoring. A water level that creeps up while the pumps run means the system is losing ground, through clogged wells, a failing pump or higher inflow than the test predicted. Treat it like a deflection trigger: a defined level that requires review, and a higher one that requires action.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is switching the pumps off on the programme date instead of the certified date. The structure may float, crack or tilt, and the damage cannot be undone.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner buys a larger pump instead of a second pump. Capacity does not help when the only pump fails at two in the morning on a Saturday.

How you will use it

Fund a pumping test. Ask every pump capacity at what head. Require N plus 1, automatic standby start, alarms that reach a person, and standby power. Do the weekend arithmetic yourself. Get the uplift crossover certified in writing and keep it on file. Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineer for permeability and drawdown; structural engineer of record for the uplift crossover.
checklist: Fund a pumping test; textbook permeability can be wrong by orders of magnitude.
Ask every quoted pump capacity: at what head?
Require N plus 1 pumps, automatic standby start, and standby power.
Make sure the alarm reaches a named person day and night.
Do the weekend arithmetic: inflow times 72 hours against excavation volume.
Confirm lawful, treated discharge of pumped water.
Never stop pumping before the engineer certifies the uplift crossover in writing.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: The programme shows dewatering ending the day after the base slab pour, to save running cost. The base sits 2 metres below the recovered water level and the slab is 0.4 metres thick. Is the date safe?
selftest.a: Almost certainly not. Two metres of head gives about 20 kilopascals of uplift, while 0.4 metres of concrete weighs only about 9.6 kilopascals, well short even before a reduced dead-load factor. Pumping must continue until the structure above adds enough weight, or the slab is anchored, and the engineer of record must certify the crossover in writing.

apply: For a hypothetical pump of 40 cubic metres an hour at 20 metres head, compute hydraulic power in kilowatts, then the motor size at 60 percent efficiency.
sources: Pump power and hydrostatic pressure are standard engineering relationships. Reduced dead-load factors for uplift follow ASCE 7 load combinations as commonly quoted [unverified — confirm independently]. Permeability ranges are general geotechnical knowledge; site values come only from testing. All figures hypothetical.

title: How a Construction Lender Reads Your Project
summary: A construction lender advances money against a building that does not yet exist, and every question he asks closes one of four gaps: ground, contractor, price and value. He sizes the loan with a few ratios, and your ground investigation and temporary works controls are credit documents to him.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a construction lender does not share your upside, so his whole method follows from wanting to be repaid, not wanting you to win. Understand his four gaps and his ratios, and you can design a package he can say yes to.

In plain English

A construction loan funds a building in stages as it is built. The lender is advancing money against a building that does not yet exist, on ground not yet proven, by a contractor who has not yet performed, at a price not yet fixed. Each of those is a gap between what he is lending against and what he can be sure of, and nearly every question he asks is an attempt to close one of them.

The four gaps

The ground gap: will the foundations cost what the budget says? He answers it with your geotechnical report, your contingency and the order in which money is spent. The contractor gap: will the builder perform? He answers it with the contractor's track record, bonds, guarantees and the contract terms. The price gap: is the budget real? He answers it with competitive bids, a cost consultant's review and the contingency. The value gap: will the finished building be worth more than the loan? He answers it with an appraisal and your income projections.

The ratios

Lenders size construction loans with a small set of ratios. All thresholds are commercial practice set by each lender and market, not law or standards; ask each prospective lender for his own.

Loan to cost compares the loan with total project cost, including land, hard and soft costs, interest and contingency. Loan to value compares it with the appraised value on completion. Debt service coverage ratio compares the building's net operating income, income after operating expenses but before debt payments, with the annual debt payments. Debt yield compares net operating income with the loan amount; it does not depend on the interest rate, so it is a cross-check that survives rate changes.

A worked example

Take a hypothetical project with total cost of 10,000,000, appraised completed value of 13,000,000 and stabilised net operating income of 800,000. Assume, purely for illustration, a lender's limits of 70 percent loan to cost, 65 percent loan to value and debt service coverage of at least 1.25.

  1. Loan to cost: 70 percent of 10,000,000 is 7,000,000.
  2. Loan to value: 65 percent of 13,000,000 is 8,450,000. Loan to cost is the tighter limit.
  3. Debt service coverage: 800,000 divided by 1.25 is 640,000 a year of maximum debt payments. If a 7,000,000 loan at the lender's rate and amortisation needs 600,000 a year, coverage is 800,000 divided by 600,000, about 1.33. It passes.
  4. What 1.25 really means: income can fall by about 20 percent, one minus one divided by 1.25, before income no longer covers the debt. It is the lender's margin for error, not your profit.
  5. Debt yield: 800,000 divided by 7,000,000 is about 11.4 percent.
  6. Equity is the gap: 10,000,000 minus 7,000,000 is 3,000,000 of your money, and lenders commonly require it to go in first.
  7. Interest during construction is a cost. If the loan averages half drawn, 3,500,000, over 2 years at a hypothetical 7 percent, that is about 490,000, and it belongs in the budget as an explicit line.

Why the ground is a credit document

Ground risk lands at the start, when the lender has advanced little and the work below ground has almost no recoverable value if the project stops. So a thin investigation does not only raise construction risk; it makes the lender require a larger contingency or more equity. Funding the investigation properly buys down the contingency he requires, and therefore the equity you must put in. Your temporary works controls tell him the same story about the riskiest months of the job.

The cash gap

Draws are paid in arrears, after work is done, inspected and certified. Between the contractor's invoice and the lender's draw there is a gap of weeks, and the owner funds it. Model it and hold working capital against it, because that gap is what kills otherwise viable projects.

How the draw works

Each month the contractor submits a payment application, the owner's representative or the lender's own monitoring surveyor checks the work in place against it, and the lender advances funds for the approved amount less retention. The lender usually checks two things at every draw: that the work claimed is really there, and that the remaining budget is enough to finish the building. If the second test fails, draws stop until the owner adds money, which is the in-balance requirement covered next week. Ask early who the lender's monitor will be and what he needs each month, because a draw delayed by missing paperwork is a cash gap the owner funds.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is approaching lenders with an incomplete package. The first submission sets the file, the analyst rebuilds your numbers from scratch, and a weak operating expense line or missing interest line becomes the lender's lasting view of the sponsor.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner negotiates the interest rate and signs whatever structure comes with it. Equity-first sequencing, contingency size, pre-leasing tests, completion guarantees, recourse and covenants often cost more than the coupon. Negotiate the structure.

How you will use it

Build your capital stack on paper first. Ask each lender for his current thresholds and design to them. Treat the geotechnical report as a credit document. Put interest during construction and the draw cash gap in the budget. Build the operating expense line from real evidence: management, reserves, insurance, utilities, standby power and maintenance. Professional sign-off required: a mortgage broker or lending adviser, an accountant, and counsel for the loan documents.
checklist: Build your capital stack on paper before approaching any lender.
Ask each lender for his current loan to cost, loan to value, coverage and debt yield thresholds.
Treat the geotechnical report as a credit document that can reduce required contingency.
Show interest during construction as an explicit budget line.
Model the cash gap between work performed and draw received, and hold working capital for it.
Build operating expenses from real evidence; the lender's analyst will rebuild them.
Negotiate the loan structure, not only the rate.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A lender's term sheet requires debt service coverage of 1.30. Your projected net operating income is 900,000. What is the maximum annual debt service, and what does the ratio protect against?
selftest.a: 900,000 divided by 1.30 is about 692,000 a year. The ratio means income could fall by about 23 percent before it stops covering the debt; it is the lender's margin for error against weaker rents or higher costs, not a measure of your profit. The threshold itself is commercial practice, set by the lender.

apply: Using your own round hypothetical numbers, compute loan to cost, loan to value, the maximum debt service at a coverage of 1.25 and the debt yield, and say which limit binds.
sources: Loan to cost, loan to value, debt service coverage and debt yield are standard commercial real estate lending measures; thresholds are commercial practice set by each lender and market, not law or standards. All figures are hypothetical. Professional advice required for any real financing.

title: Week Four Review: The Hole, the Water and the Lender
summary: Six scenario questions on excavation protection, sloped versus shored volumes, dewatering and uplift, and how a lender sizes a construction loan. The week's thread is that the first months on site are the riskiest for everyone, including the lender.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this week followed the first money into the ground: the rules that keep people safe in the hole, the shape that sets its volume, the water that must come out, and the lender watching all of it. Work each question aloud before reading the answer.

Question 1. A trench is 1.8 metres deep in firm clay with no seepage, and the foreman says it does not need protection because the clay is stiff. Is he right?

Answer. Not on that basis. Under OSHA Subpart P as commonly quoted, protection is required unless the excavation is in stable rock or less than about 1.5 metres deep with a competent person finding no indication of cave-in (verify against the current regulation). At 1.8 metres, a protective system is needed: sloping or benching to the soil type, a support system, or a shield. Stiffness is not an exemption.

Question 2. You see a loaded excavator working at the lip of a sloped excavation, with a spoil heap beside it. You are working under Design-Build. What do you do?

Answer. Observe, photograph and write. Ask the contractor to confirm in writing that the loading is within the temporary works design and the competent person's inspection. Do not instruct the operator or direct the method, because directing method moves temporary works responsibility back onto you. Load at the crest is a common contributing cause of collapse, so ask now, not at the next meeting.

Question 3. A footprint of 30 by 20 metres plus 1 metre working space is dug 2 metres deep. What is the shored volume, and roughly how many 10 cubic metre loads at a bulking factor of 1.25?

Answer. The base is 32 by 22 metres, 704 square metres, times 2 is 1,408 cubic metres in the ground. Loose volume is 1,408 times 1.25, which is 1,760 cubic metres, or 176 truck loads. At 24 loads a day through one gate that is about 7 to 8 days, whatever size excavator is on site.

Question 4. A dewatering subcontractor quotes a pump at 50 cubic metres an hour. What is the one question to ask?

Answer. At what head? A pump's flow falls as the head it lifts against rises, so the duty point is flow and head together. Then ask about the standby pump, automatic start, the alarm, standby power and the discharge permit.

Question 5. The base slab will sit 3 metres below the recovered water level. How much concrete thickness balances the uplift, before any factor?

Answer. Three metres of head is about 30 kilopascals. At about 24 kilonewtons per cubic metre, that needs 30 divided by 24, about 1.25 metres of concrete, and more once only a reduced share of dead load is counted. Pumping continues until the structure above supplies the shortfall, or the slab is anchored, and the engineer certifies the crossover in writing before any pump stops.

Question 6. Your project shows net operating income of 750,000 and the lender requires coverage of 1.25. Your proposed loan needs 640,000 a year of debt service. Does it pass, and what does the ratio mean?

Answer. 750,000 divided by 640,000 is about 1.17, which fails. The maximum debt service at 1.25 is 600,000 a year, so the loan must be smaller or the terms longer. A coverage of 1.25 means income can fall about 20 percent before it fails to cover the debt; it is the lender's margin for error, and the threshold is commercial practice, not a standard.

Recap

Excavation protection is workplace safety law. In American practice OSHA Subpart P requires a protective system in most excavations: sloping or benching, support, or shields, with engineer design beyond the depth threshold. Soil type decides slopes, and seeping soil is Type C. Where the slope does not fit inside the boundary, shoring is a geometry decision.

The owner walks the crest first, then the base, the water and the paperwork, and under Design-Build observes and asks rather than directs.

A shored hole is base area times depth; a sloped hole uses the prismoidal formula and is much larger. The extra volume costs haulage, backfill, dewatering and days, and haulage, not digging, sets the duration.

Dewatering is sized from a pumping test, bought at a duty point of flow and head, and arranged with redundancy, alarms and standby power. It stops only when the engineer certifies the uplift crossover.

A lender closes four gaps, ground, contractor, price and value, and sizes the loan with loan to cost, loan to value, debt service coverage and debt yield. The ground investigation is a credit document, interest during construction is a cost, and the draw cash gap needs working capital.

The thread: the first months on site carry the most uncertainty and the least recoverable value, for the owner and the lender alike, and the controls you put on the hole are the same controls the lender reads in your file. Professional sign-off required: temporary works designer, geotechnical engineer, structural engineer of record, and lending and legal advisers.

Notice how often this week's answers were a question rather than an instruction: at what head, at what bulking factor, at what threshold, certified by whom. On the site and at the bank alike, the owner's strongest move is usually the precise question asked early, in writing, of the person who is responsible for the answer.

Next week stays with the money. A building can be finished on time and to specification and still be lost, and the lessons ahead show how: thin equity, the wrong debt, a foundation surprise that trips a covenant, and a partner who must agree before anything is paid.
checklist: Require a protective system in every excavation beyond the regulatory exemption.
Observe, record and ask at the crest; do not direct method under Design-Build.
Add working space and bulking before counting trucks.
Ask every pump quote for its head and its standby arrangement.
Stop pumping only on a written uplift-crossover certificate.
Test every loan against the lender's own coverage and cost ratios.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: Why does a lender care about your dewatering and temporary works controls?
selftest.a: Because the excavation and foundation months carry the highest uncertainty while the work done has almost no recoverable value if the project stops. Strong controls lower the chance of a costly surprise when the lender's position is weakest, which can reduce the contingency or equity he requires.
